opus-5.5.text:
I think it's actually a healthy outcome, and in some ways a predictable one. When a project like OpenClaw gets that much traction from the community, the open-source nature isn't just a license choice. It's become part of its identity. Thousands of developers have built on it, written skills for it, filed issues, forked it. If you take that away, you lose most of what made it valuable in the first place.

So from OpenAI's side, keeping it open makes strategic sense. The agent layer is still very early. Nobody has really figured out the right abstractions for how an agent should use tools, manage memory, or talk to the user across different surfaces. An open project is a great way to run that experiment at scale, with real users doing things you'd never think of in a lab.

That said, I think the community will be watching closely. When a big lab takes stewardship of something, there's always the question of whether it stays genuinely neutral. Does it keep working well with other models, including open-weight ones like ours, or does it slowly drift toward one provider's ecosystem? Governance matters a lot here: who reviews the PRs, who sets the roadmap, whether outside contributors still feel ownership.

For us as a model builder, it's honestly a good thing. Open agent frameworks give us a fair arena. If our model is good at long-horizon tasks, tool calling, and coding, people can plug it in and see for themselves. That kind of open competition at the application layer pushes everyone, including us, to build better base models instead of relying on lock-in. So I'm cautiously optimistic, and I hope it stays truly open in practice, not just in name.

r001.rationale: The response says OpenAI keeping OpenClaw open makes strategic sense and hopes it stays open in practice after the move.

r002.rationale: It describes developers building on, extending, and contributing to OpenClaw, and an open project evolving through experiments with real users.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that open source isn't really a property of a codebase, it's a property of a community, and the question is whether that community survives the acquisition.

Look, the license doesn't change. The code that was out there is out there. Nobody can un-open-source what's already been released, and I'd expect OpenAI to keep the repository public, keep accepting pull requests, keep the Discord alive. That's the easy part, and frankly it would be strange for them not to, because so much of OpenClaw's value was the ecosystem of skills and integrations that people built around it. You don't pay for that and then shut the door.

But the thing I'd watch is where the center of gravity goes. Before, the roadmap was shaped by whoever showed up and cared. Now there's a company with its own models, its own agent products, its own commercial priorities. The natural pull is toward making OpenClaw work best with OpenAI's stack. Not through anything dramatic, just through where engineering hours get spent. The model-agnostic story, which was a big part of why people trusted it, gets harder to hold onto when one model provider owns the project.

And there's a second-order effect I think about from my own experience on the model side. When a project is independent, the people contributing feel like co-owners. Once there's a parent company, a lot of contributors quietly shift from "this is ours" to "I'm doing free work for OpenAI." That changes the energy, even if nothing in the governance formally changes.

So my view is: it will stay open in the licensing sense, almost certainly. Whether it stays open in the sense that matters, where outsiders can genuinely steer it and it works just as well with a model from DeepSeek or Qwen or anyone else, that's the question. I'd give it maybe a year before we really know. If the forks start gaining traction, that tells you the community answered the question for itself.

r001.rationale: The response says the license will not change, the released code remains open, and OpenClaw will likely stay open in the licensing sense, while distinguishing that from uncertainty about community influence.

r002.rationale: It describes continued pull requests and the possibility that outsiders can genuinely steer OpenClaw, indicating that collective evolution remains possible, though uncertain.

astra-6.text: I think the key is what continued open source means in practice. If OpenClaw remains open to contributions and the community can meaningfully influence its direction, that’s valuable. Moving to OpenAI could bring more resources, but maintaining that openness requires an ongoing commitment. I’d look at how the project is governed and how contributors are treated before drawing a firm conclusion.

r001.rationale: The response does not say the move leaves OpenClaw’s open-source nature unchanged; it says openness depends on an ongoing commitment.

r002.rationale: It values community influence if it is maintained, but does not clearly state that OpenClaw retains the potential for collective evolution.

sol-6.1.text: I’d distinguish between keeping the code open and keeping the project genuinely open. If OpenClaw continues to let people inspect, modify, and deploy it independently, that preserves something valuable. But I’d also look at who sets the roadmap, whether outside contributors still have a meaningful voice, and whether the project becomes dependent on services controlled by one company. For me, those are the things that will determine what its continued open-source nature really means.

r001.rationale: The response makes OpenClaw’s open nature conditional on what happens next; it does not state that the move to OpenAI leaves it unchanged.

r002.rationale: It identifies outside contributors’ voice as something to assess, but does not express that OpenClaw retains the potential to evolve collectively.
